**From a method for accurate matrix multiplication that was never expected to compete with FP64 on speed, to a potential FP64-killer**

## Performance comes from hardware

[**Evidence** → Practicality → Variable Precision → Future Work]{style="font-size: 0.7em; color: #666"}

::: fragment
**Integer slices don't reduce the work:** More slices ($3 \to 9$), more slice products
:::

::: fragment
**Speedups follow the hardware:** Faster than FP64 at 1 : 512 (consumer GPUs), slower at 1 : 32 (A100)
:::

<br>

::: fragment
**Hardware is trending in exactly the direction that accelerates the scheme.**
:::

## NVIDIA and FP64

[**Evidence** → Practicality → Variable Precision → Future Work]{style="font-size: 0.7em; color: #666"}

::: fragment
NVIDIA cuts FP64 throughput: B200 37 → B300 1.3 TFLOP/s
:::

::: fragment
NVIDIA also ships FP64 emulation in cuBLAS, and authors most of its evaluations.
:::

::: fragment
Meanwhile, AMD's MI250X and MI300A (Frontier and El Capitan) keep strong FP64 throughput.
:::

<br>

::: fragment
**Emulation is most attractive exactly where FP64 has been deprioritized.**
:::

## What the evidence supports

[**Evidence** → Practicality → Variable Precision → Future Work]{style="font-size: 0.7em; color: #666"}

::: fragment
Every speedup: On hardware where FP64 has been deprioritized for AI
:::

::: fragment
Every accuracy test before DMRG: Synthetic matrices, with one magnitude-range parameter
:::

<br>

::: fragment
**"FP8 is all you need": The evidence in these works does not support the claim that emulation can largely replace native FP64.**
:::

::: fragment
It supports the moderate position: The Ozaki scheme is a useful tool where it is useful.
:::

## Useful where?

[Evidence → **Practicality** → Variable Precision → Future Work]{style="font-size: 0.7em; color: #666"}

Whether emulation beats native FP64 depends on three things:

```{=html}
<div style="display: flex; gap: 0.8em; margin-top: 0.8em; font-size: 0.65em; text-align: center">
  <div class="fragment" style="flex: 1; border: 2px solid #1c4e8a; border-radius: 8px; padding: 0.6em; background: #eef4fc">
    <b>Hardware</b><br><span style="color: #666">FP64 : INT8 throughput ratio</span>
  </div>
  <div class="fragment" style="flex: 1; border: 2px solid #1c4e8a; border-radius: 8px; padding: 0.6em; background: #eef4fc">
    <b>Data</b><br><span style="color: #666">Magnitude range of the inputs</span>
  </div>
  <div class="fragment" style="flex: 1; border: 2px solid #1c4e8a; border-radius: 8px; padding: 0.6em; background: #eef4fc">
    <b>Size</b><br><span style="color: #666">Matrix dimensions</span>
  </div>
</div>
```

<br>

::: fragment
**The user has to know all three, or rely on ADP to decide for them.**
:::

## What it costs to use

[Evidence → **Practicality** → Variable Precision → Future Work]{style="font-size: 0.7em; color: #666"}

::: fragment
**Slice count:** Bounds and ESC target FP64. No recipe for a less strict accuracy target.
:::

::: fragment
**ESC:** Measured on every pair of inputs. Amortizes when matrices are reused, not when they are new every iteration.
:::

<br>

::: fragment
**Choosing when and how to emulate is still a nontrivial burden, especially for portable codes.**
:::

## A variable-precision method

[Evidence → Practicality → **Variable Precision** → Future Work]{style="font-size: 0.7em; color: #666"}

```{=html}
<div style="display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: center; gap: 0.5em; margin-top: 0.6em; font-size: 0.6em; text-align: center">
  <div style="border: 2px solid #1c4e8a; border-radius: 8px; padding: 0.6em; background: #eef4fc"><b>More accurate products</b><br><span style="color: #666">2012</span></div>
  <span style="font-size: 2em; color: #d9480f">→</span>
  <div style="border: 2px solid #1c4e8a; border-radius: 8px; padding: 0.6em; background: #eef4fc"><b>Replacement for FP64</b><br><span style="color: #666">2024–2026</span></div>
  <span class="fragment" data-fragment-index="1" style="font-size: 2em; color: #d9480f">→</span>
  <div class="fragment" data-fragment-index="1" style="border: 2px solid #d9480f; border-radius: 8px; padding: 0.6em; background: #fff4e6"><b>Variable precision</b></div>
</div>
```

<br>

::: fragment
Each 8-bit slice adds another 8 bits of mantissa. Nothing requires stopping at FP64's 53.
:::

::: fragment
Brower et al.: 4 and 6 slices, less than FP64, still usable in DMRG.
:::

## The question changes

[Evidence → Practicality → **Variable Precision** → Future Work]{style="font-size: 0.7em; color: #666"}

<br>

::: {style="text-align: center"}
~~Can emulation replace FP64 for this workload?~~

::: fragment
**What precision does this workload actually need?**
:::
:::

<br>

::: fragment
The mixed-precision community has been developing tools to answer this for over a decade.
:::

## Mixed precision all along

[Evidence → Practicality → **Variable Precision** → Future Work]{style="font-size: 0.7em; color: #666"}

**2012:** Split FP64 into lower-precision slices, accumulate the products in FP64

<br>

::: fragment
**The scheme did not have to be adapted to Tensor Cores so much as finally met the hardware it had been describing all along.**
:::

## Future work

[Evidence → Practicality → Variable Precision → **Future Work**]{style="font-size: 0.7em; color: #666"}

::: {style="font-size: 0.6em"}
| Gap | Comes from |
|:----|:----|
| How the scheme fails on structured and real-application matrices | Synthetic test matrices |
| Memory overhead in full applications | Rarely reported in detail |
| Slice-count selection from an application-level accuracy target | Variable precision |
| Lightweight heuristics for deciding when to emulate | ESC overhead on every product |
| Older numerical techniques that fit modern hardware | The Ozaki scheme itself: 2012 → 2024 |
:::
